speaker: jaycohen
text: Well, good morning. Welcome to an oral argument session of the Fifth District Court of Appeal. I'm Jay Cohen. Joining me on the panel today, we've got Judge John Harris from Brevard County and Judge Karianne Wozniak from Orange County. We've got one Zoom and we're going to go into the courtroom for the rest of the oral arguments this morning. The case we have first is Boulder 3 LLC et al. versus Buffalo Ridge Property Owners Association et al. Case number 21909. Each side will be entitled up to 20 minutes each for their presentation. We have a default of five minutes for rebuttal, but if you'd like something different, all you have to do is just let me know and I'll be glad to accommodate whatever time that you'd like. That said, counsel for appellant, you may proceed.

speaker: richardhennings
text: Morning, Your Honors. I'm Richard Hennings. I'm from Eustis, the law firm of Richard W. Hennings, PA. I represent Boulder 3 and also a corporation called MacWiff. I will refer to that corporation as Mac and I'll refer to Boulder as Boulder. These are, for purposes of appeal, are consolidated because I had filed a notice of related issues. The facts are, I think, fairly simple in this case. In 2013, Mac purchased by tax day property, which I'll describe as the north parking lot in the Palm Ridge Plaza. In 2018, Boulder purchased the south parking lot by tax deed. I believe the Boulder tax deed, we paid $182,000 for it. The Mac tax deed, I believe we paid $69,000 for it. This case really involves a statutory interpretation of one particular statute and actually only about three or four lines out of that statute. Unfortunately, I'm not able to find any case that interprets the statute the way that we're talking about today. I don't believe counsel has found any specific case directly on point. The statute that we're talking about is Florida Statute 197.573. Tax deeds, of course, are handled differently than, let's say, non-tax deeds such as warranty deeds or trustee deeds in the sense that tax deeds, once they're issued, the legislature basically says what survives that tax deed and what does not survive the tax deed. The most obvious example is mortgages. If there's a mortgage on the record, then a tax deed will wipe out that mortgage. What we're dealing with today, though, is not a mortgage but with covenants and restrictions that are in a declaration, which was recorded in 2005, which I'll refer to as the Buffalo Ridge Declaration. The Buffalo Ridge Declaration contains various covenants and restrictions. Our position is that the covenants and restrictions of Buffalo Ridge did not survive the tax deed within the meaning of Florida Statute 197.573. We believe that the statute is unambiguous in what it provides. We also will be talking about the fact that that statute was amended in 2018, which has led to an argument by Buffalo Ridge's council that the amended statute applies. But prior to the amendment, 197.573 had this language in the first part of it. When a deed in the chain of title contains restrictions and covenants running with the land, the restrictions and covenants survive the tax deed.

speaker: wozniak
text: And here, the previous deed, it did reference any restrictions and all that. That was mentioned in the deeds, correct?

speaker: richardhennings
text: The 2000, we're not talking about the tax deed right now. We're talking about a Boulder acquired, excuse me, the original owner of this property, being the Palm Ridge Plaza Property Owners Association, acquired the property in 2007. Mack also, excuse me, Palm Ridge Plaza also acquired the property by special warranty deed in 2007. It's just that one was for the north parking lot, one was for the south parking lot. It was because Palm Ridge Plaza, the original owner, did not pay the property taxes that eventually led to the tax deeds. But both of those warranty deeds are virtually identical, with the exception that the grantors are different. The grantees are the same. The Palm Ridge Plaza Property Owners Association. Both deeds do make specific reference to a different declaration, which is a declaration that is still in litigation in this particular case, that being what I call the Palm Ridge Declaration.

speaker: wozniak
text: Well, the deeds also say subject to covenants, easements, and restrictions of record, if any, correct? Yes, ma'am. Say that, okay. So, and that's not enough, and it's your position that that's not enough for the declaration to still apply.

speaker: richardhennings
text: And yes, ma'am, that's correct. And the reason that we do not believe that the declaration still applies under that particular general reservation is because, I mean, I would agree that if we were talking about a warranty deed, we were talking about a trustee's deed, or one of those non-tax deeds that the Buffalo Ridge Declaration would be incorporated into deed. But we're not talking about a non-tax deed. We're talking about a deed that is affected specifically by Florida Statute 197.573. And what that statute said before the amendment was that the covenants and restrictions had to be contained within the deed. It wasn't until 2018 that the statute was amended to say deeds or other recorded instruments. So, the covenants and restrictions...

speaker: jaycohen
text: Mr. Higgs, what does the word contained mean in the earlier version of the statute?

speaker: richardhennings
text: I believe the word contained means that the covenants and restrictions have to be within, I mean, the word contained means within, have to be contained within the deed itself. Can't they be contained within by reference? The statute does not say that. And to that particular point, Your Honor, I think the legislature, I don't see any legislative history on this statute either. The legislature perhaps recognized that the pre-2018 amendment just said it contained within the deed. And so in 2018, they said, well, it also includes other recorded instruments. And our position is that the Buffalo Ridge Declaration is an other recorded instrument. And so if we were talking about tax deeds that were affected by the amendment, then it would include other recorded instruments. But the fact that the pre-2018 statute did not use the term other recorded instruments, I think, indicates to me that other recorded instruments like the Buffalo Ridge Declaration would not be included in a tax deed that was not affected by the 2018 amendment. So again, to summarize, I believe that prior to the amendment, the covenants and restrictions had to be contained in the deed itself. And there are no covenants and restrictions contained in the 2007 deeds, which were in the chain of title. There's only a reference to them. And the statute that we have at issue here does not include the pre-2018 statute does not include other recorded instruments, such as the Buffalo Ridge Declaration. It doesn't even include the Palm Ridge Declaration, which is not an issue here, but it certainly doesn't include the Buffalo Ridge Declaration, which isn't even mentioned in the 2007 warranty deeds. If the declaration had been mentioned, if it said

speaker: wozniak
text: Buffalo Ridge Declaration, would that have been enough or would it have actually had to list every single item that's in the declaration under your position? Well, under our position

speaker: richardhennings
text: and under what we believe is the unambiguous language of the statute, the actual covenants and restrictions would have been included in the deed. And many deeds, so not so much with your more modern deeds, but certainly with your less modern deeds, it was quite common to include restrictions and covenants in the deed itself. And in fact, you still see some of those deeds like that. And that may have been the reason that the legislature amended the statute in 2018 to include other recorded instruments, which would at that point would include declarations in the chain of title that were simply referenced by the terms subject to covenants and restrictions and easements of record, but not in the pre-2018 amendment. I believe that the covenants and restrictions must be included in the deed. Now, there's no question that the MAC deed is not subject to the 2018 amendment. The MAC deed was issued in 2013, several years before the amendment. There's a question that's been raised by the Buffalo Ridge Council that, well, the Boulder deed is covered by the 2018 amendment. We would disagree with that because if you look at, which is part of the record, if you look at section 60 of laws of Florida 2018-118, which talks about the effective date of the statute, section 60 says that the amendments made by this act to 197.573 first apply to taxes and special assessments levied in 2018. And our position is that even though the Boulder deed was issued about four months after July of 2018, that if you look at section 60 that says that the amendment to 197.573 first applies to taxes levied in 2018, the Boulder deed would not have been issued with respect to 2018 taxes. Now, there's nothing in the record to indicate what taxes were not paid prior to the issuance of the 2018 Boulder deed. But because if you look at the deed on the face of it, it says it was issued pursuant to a tax certificate issued in 2012. But of course, under the statutes, if you're going to bid on property at a tax deed sale, you have to pay not only the amount that was owed on, in this case, the 2012 taxes, but you have to pay all the taxes that accrued subsequent to that. And if you assume that the 2017 taxes were not paid, then that would have been included in the amount that Boulder had to pay when it bid up the tax deed sale. The Boulder tax deed was issued in, I believe it was October of 2018. And of course, the 2018 taxes would not have even been due at that particular time. The only taxes that would have been levied at that point would have been the 2017 taxes. So for that reason, we do not believe that the 2018 amendment to the statute applies to the Boulder tax deed. There was some discussion by the lower court. There was also some discussion in the answer brief about the marketable record title act. Not really sure why that act was brought into this case because I think that the survival of the covenants and restrictions is totally determined by 197.573. MARTA is just a general statute that applies to all deeds. And it basically says, if you got a deed that's 30 or more years old, you might be able to wipe out covenants and restrictions that are fairly old, fairly ancient. But of course, under 197.573, if the covenants and restrictions do not survive, I mean, they're wiped out immediately. You don't have to rely upon MARTA. So I don't really know why MARTA was brought in, but it was brought in.
